Root_Function: The suffix -lessattaches primarily to monosyllabic English nouns. However, -lessis a fully productive suffix, meaning it can be added to any noun to form legitimate new words.
The prefix syl-occurs in Greek loanwords and hence attaches to Greek bases. It is an assimilated form of syn-used before roots beginning with l, such as "log". See syn-.
The suffix -en2forms adjectives from monosyllabic native English nouns denoting material or source

Root_Definition: to go; to go back or yield

Root_Function: The prefix "syn-" occurs in Greek loanwords and attaches to Greek roots. It has several forms, as the final "n" sound in "syn-" assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See its assimilated forms sym-, syl-, and sys-.
The suffix -aciousforms adjectives from Latinate nouns ending in "-acity," "-acy," or "-ce." Most common adjectives ending in -acioushave a corresponding noun form ending in "-acity."

Root_Definition: the act, process, or result of
Root_Function: The suffix -ionattaches to bases that are Latin verb stems ending in s or t.

Root_Definition: excessively, too much; over, on top, above

Root_Function: The suffix -al1attaches to verbs, primarily verbs from Latin or from Latin via French, to form nouns. The base verb always has primary stress on its final syllable.

Root_Name: op, ops, opt, opto, ophthalm, ophthalmo, -opia, -opsy
Root_Definition: eye, visual condition, vision, sight, inspection
to cover or surround with; to act on or change another.
Root_Function: The prefix be-forms verbs from nouns and verbs.
The prefix "sur-" occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of "sub-" used before roots beginning with "r." See sub-.
The prefix o-is an assimilated form of ob-.

Root_Definition: from; away from; down from; reverse, negate.
characterized by; full of; tending to
Root_Function: The suffix -y1, -eyattaches to nouns and a few verbs to form adjectives.

Root_Definition: in a state or condition (produced by the action denoted by the verb base)
Root_Function: The suffix -ite1attaches to Latin roots, as most English adjectives ending in -ite1are loanwords from Latin, specifically from past participles of verbs formed with the suffix -itus.

The suffix -ateprimarily forms transitive verbs from Latin bases.  Many -ateverbs were loanwords from Latin.  Verbs ending in -atecombine with the suffix -ion to form nouns ending in -ation. These verbs also have corresponding agent nouns ending in -ator (navigator, dictator, elevator).
The prefix "sum-" occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of "sub-" used before  roots beginning with "m." See sub-
The prefix as-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with an "s" sound, such as "sent" and "cert." See ad-.

Root_Synonyms: magn, magna, magni, maxi, mega, megal, megalo, -megaly

Root_Definition: to turn into or cause to be
Root_Function: The suffix -ize, -iseforms transitive verbs from adjectives (civilize) and nouns (crystallize). The oldest English verbs ending in -izewere loanwords from Greek (baptize, catechize).

Root_Definition: on, upon, over; beyond, after, outside
science, study, or practice of; properties of; practices pertaining to
the act, process, or result of
Root_Function: The suffix -ationis a compound of -ate1+ -ion. It turns verbs ending in -ate into nouns (decorate/ decoration). Not all nouns with this suffix, however, have a corresponding verb ending in -ate (information, alteration).
See also -logy, -ology, a terminal form of this root.
The suffix -ly2attaches primarily to native English nouns to form adjectives.

Root_Definition: person who does or believes in
Root_Function: Many words ending in -isthave a corresponding abstract noun form ending in -ism, and many have a corresponding adjective form ending in -ic (realistic, artistic).
The prefix ef-is an assimilated form of the prefix ex-, used before roots beginning with f, such as "fac" and "fus." See ex-.
See also fer, lat2, -late

Root_Definition: down; completely, thoroughly; against; according to

Root_Function: This root is also the origin of the suffixes "-fy, -ify, -efy" and "-ification, -efaction".
The prefix con-is an assimilated form of com-used before roots beginning with c, d, f, g, j, n, s, t, and v. See com-. Note: con-is frequently an intensive prefix, as in "conceive."

Root_Definition: in the manner or way indicated by the adjective
Root_Function: Adjectives with the suffix -able or -ible are turned into adverbs by dropping the final e and adding -ly1.

Root_Definition: a person, thing, or place associated with
one who does or is related to

Root_Function: The prefix ag-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with "g." See ad-.
The prefix at-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with "t," such as "tract" and "ten, tin, tain." See ad-.
The prefix es-is an assimilated form of the prefix ex-, used before roots beginning with a hard "c". See ex-.
The suffix -mentattaches to Latin verb roots (e.g., doc, reg, sed) or to English verbs of Latin origin to form nouns.

The prefix sub-was a Latin preposition and prefix and occurs in English in Latin loanwords, such as subjugate. It is also used in the formation of English words such as subwayand subgroup. It has multiple forms, as the 'b' sound in sub-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See the assimilated forms suc-, suf-, sum-, sup-, sur-, sus-, and su-.
The prefix e-is an assimilated form of ex-used before roots beginning with certain consonants (b d, g, j, l, m, n, r, v). See ex-.
The suffix -ful2attaches to native English nouns denoting containers to form amount nouns.

The prefix com-attaches to Latin bases beginning with m, p, or b. It has multiple forms, as the 憁' sound in com-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See the assimilated forms col-, con-, cor-, and co-. Note: com-is frequently an intensive prefix, as in "commemorate" and "command."
The prefix ac-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before Latin roots beginning with hard or soft "c" or "q." See ad-.
The suffix -ureattaches to Latin verb roots and English verbs.
The  prefix op-is an assimilated form of ob-used before roots beginning with "p," such as "pos." See ob-.

Root_ID: wrd_cur1, curr, cor1, corr, curs, cour1, cours
Root_Name: cur1, curr, cor1, corr, curs, cour1, cours

Root_Definition: across, over, to the other side
capable of being, doing, or undergoing
Root_Function: The suffix -able, and its variants, is attached to Latin verb roots or English transitive verbs to form adjectives. (In a small set of cases, -ableis attached to a noun, e.g. knowledgeable and marriageable.)  For spelling purposes, it is useful to know that -ableis more likely to be added to a whole English word (comparable, adorable), while -ibleis more likely to follow a bound root (visible, legible). However,there are still many words which combine a root with -able(capable, inevitable).  The suffix -ity can be added to any adjective ending in -able, -ible, -bleto produce a corresponding noun ending in -ability, -ibility, -bility (possible+ -ity > possibility; irrevocable+ -ity > irrevocability.)
The prefix ig-occurs in Latin loanwords and in words formed using Latin roots. It is an assimilated form of in-2used before roots beginning with "n," such as "nom." See in-2.
The suffix -osisattaches to Greek roots. Many nouns ending in "-osis" have a corresponding adjective form ending in -otic (neurosis: neurotic).

Root_Definition: one believing in; one associated with; one having (age)

Root_Function: Most words containing the prefix ab-, abs-are Latin loanwords, so the bases are Latin roots. ab-becomes abs-before bases beginning with "t," such as "tract."

Root_Definition: ability to do, be, or undergo
Root_Function: All adjectives ending in "-able," "-ible,"   "-uble" and "-ble" can combine with the suffix "-ity" to form nouns ending in -ability, -ibility, -ubility, or -bility.
The prefix af-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with "f," such as fil1and fix.  See ad-.

The prefix sym-occurs in Greek loanwords and hence attaches to Greek bases. It is an assimilated form of syn-used before roots beginning with b, p, and m, such as "bio, bi, -be", "path, patho, -pathic, -pathy", and "metr, -meter, -metry". See syn-and its other assimilated forms syl-and sys-.
The prefix ar-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with "r," such as "rang." See ad-.

Root_Synonyms: magn, magna, magni, mega, megal, megalo, -megaly, macro-

Root_Definition: in such a way or manner
Root_Function: The suffix -ly1turns adjectives into adverbs. It attaches to most English adjectives to form legitimate words. However, adjectives derived from identical nouns (yellow, chocolate) will generally sound nonsensical.

Root_Definition: tending to, connected with, or performing
Root_Function: The suffix -ive, -ativeturns Latinate verb bases into adjectives. Many adjectives ending in -ive, -ativehave corresponding noun forms ending in -ity (objective, objectivity) or -ion (effusive, effusion).

Root_Synonyms: ec, ect, ecto, ex-, extr-, extra-, exter-

Root_Function: The prefix of-is an assimilated form of ob-used before roots beginning with "f." See ob-.

Root_Synonyms: prim, princ, arch, archi, arche (archae), archeo, (archaeo), -arch, -archy

Root_Definition: (in adjectives) doing the action denoted by the verb root; (in nouns) one who or that which does the action denoted by the verb root.
Root_Function: The suffix -ant, -entforms adjectives and, to a much lesser extent, nouns from Latin verb stems such as fid in confidentand stud in student. This suffix is the equivalent in Latin of the "-ing" inflection in English. Many adjectives ending in -ant, -enthave a corresponding noun ending in -ance, -ence, -ancy, -ency.

Root_Antonyms: magn, magna, magni, maxi, mega, megal, megalo, -megaly, macro-

Root_Definition: to turn; to be occupied with

Root_Function: The suffix -ful1attaches to native English nouns to form adjectives.

Root_Definition: having many or much of; tending toward
Root_Function: Adjectives ending in -ose1were borrowed as whole words from Latin, where the suffix was -osus. The suffix -ose1is therefore always attached to a bound Latin root. Most adjectives ending in -ose1have a corresponding noun form ending in -ity (verbose: verbosity). See -osity.
The suffix -izationturns verbs ending in -ize into nouns

Root_Definition: similar to, in the manner of
Root_Function: The suffix -likeattaches primarily to English nouns to form adjectives.

Root_Definition: resembling, related to, made of, or, in biological science, belonging to (a taxonomic class)
Root_Function: The suffix -aceousoccurs in adjectives that are Latin loanwords, and hence attaches to Latin noun roots. Words ending in -aceousare often formal and used  in biological science. These scientific adjectives ending in -aceoushave corresponding nouns ending in -aceae (plants) and -acea (animals), which are names for taxonomic families.
The suffix -ary1attaches to Latin roots (e.g., primary, literary) and to nouns (e.g., cautionary, fragmentary), forming adjectives.

Root_Definition: in adjectives: from (a place) or pertaining to or following (a figure or school of thought); in nouns: person or thing from (a place) or associated with (an activity or school of thought).
Root_Function: The suffix group -an, -ian, -eanattaches to common nouns and proper nouns to form adjectives or nouns.

The prefix dis-occurs in English attached to Latin roots, as in dissent, but also forms words in English by attaching to verbs (dishearten) and nouns (disbelief). dis-has two other forms, as the "s" sound  in dis-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See the assimilated forms dif-and di-3.
The suffix "-tude" attaches to Latin roots.
The suffix -ficoccurs in adjectives that are Latin loanwords, and hence attaches to bases that are Latin noun roots. It is a form of "fer, lat2, -late".
The prefix sup-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of sub-used before roots that begin with "p," such as "port." See sub-

The suffix group -fy, -ify, -efyforms verbs from primarily Latin bases.  When -ifyattaches to an English base, the base is an adjective (uglify, Frenchify) or noun (citify, zombify) usually having one syllable or two syllables ending in |i|. Verbs ending in -fyhave corresponding noun forms ending in -ion: as a rule, -ifybecomes -ification (verify, verification); -efybecomes -efaction (putrefy, putrefaction). See also fac, fic, fec, fact, fect.

Root_Definition: act, process, or result of (the action indicated by the verb base)
Root_Function: The suffix -ageattaches primarily to bases that are English verbs to form nouns. Base-final y becomes i and base-final silent e is dropped before 朼ge (carry + -age> carriage, store + -age> storage) Some nouns ending in -ageare loan words from French (voyage, courage) whose bases are Latin roots.

Root_Definition: study of, science of; written work; structure or principle
Root_Function: The suffix -logy, -ologyforms nouns from bases that are predominantly Greek roots. It is a terminal form of the root log, logo, -loguewhich in the vast majority cases signifies the study or science of the subject  indicated by the base. In some words, however, -ologycarries the meaning "written work" (trilogy) or "structure" (homology). See log, logo, -logue. Most nouns ending in -logy, -ologyhave an adjective form ending in "-ical." (dermatology, dermatological).

Root_Definition: a person or thing that does
Root_Function: The suffix -atorturns verbs ending in -ate into nouns. It is a compound of -ate + -or.

The prefix co-is a reduced form of com-often used before roots beginning with vowels, such as "ax" and "ev." It is also used with existing English words to indicate a role of fellowship (coworker) or that something is done together (cowrite)  See com-.

The suffix -nessis attached to adjectives to form nouns. It is fully productive, meaning that any word that combines an adjective and the suffix -nessis an allowable English noun.  In a small set of cases, it is attached to a verb (forgiveness) or a noun (witness).
The prefix cor-is an assimilated form of com-used before roots beginning with "r." See com-.

Root_Definition: out, outside, outward; beyond, better, more
having the nature of, characterized by
Root_Function: The suffix -itiousattaches to Latin roots to form adjectives.
The suffix -al2, -ialattaches primarily to nouns (national, environmental) but sometimes to Latin or Greek roots (final, capital, comical) to form adjectives. See also -ar1.

Root_Definition: act, process, state, practice, or instance of
Root_Function: The suffix -ism1attaches to Greek roots to form nouns which usually have a corresponding verb ending in "-ize, -ise". See also -ism2.
The prefix ap-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with "p." See ad-.

The prefix "sys-" occurs in Greek loanwords and hence attaches to Greek bases. It is an assimilated form of "syn-" used before roots beginning with s. See syn-and its other assimilated forms syl-and sym-.
The prefix col-is an assimilated form of com-used before roots beginning with "l," such as "loc" and "lect." See com-.

In Latin, "extrem" is the superlative form of "exter," just as in English "most" is the superlative form of "more." "Extrem," which is the basis of the basis of the English word "extreme" and its derivations, thus means "most outside" or "most beyond."
The prefix "su-" occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of "sub-."

Root_Definition: in adjectives: of or pertaining to; resembling; in nouns: someone afflicted with;
Root_Function: The suffix -acattaches to Greek bases ending in the letter "i" to form adjectives and their noun extensions. Many English adjectives ending in -acare loanwords from Greek via Latin. However, later words such as "dipsomaniac" are new English words modeled on loanwords.
The prefix dif-is an assimilated form of the prefix dis-, used before roots beginning with "f", such as "fid" and "fer." See dis-.

Root_Antonyms: magn, magna, magni, maxi, mega, megal, megalo, -megaly, macro-

Root_Function: The suffix -domattaches to primarily Old English adjectives and nouns.

Root_Definition: act or process of making or becoming
Root_Function: The suffix -ification, -efactionforms nouns from verbs ending in -ify, -efy, -fy. It is a compound of fac, fic, fec, fact, fect + -ion.  The -fy and -efy forms become -efaction(stupefy, stupefaction); -ify becomes -ification(magnify, magnification).

Root_Definition: capable of being or undergoing; pertaining to

Root_Function: The prefix ex-was a Latin preposition and prefix and occurs in English in Latin loanwords, such as exitand expel.  It has multiple forms, as the 'x' sound in ex-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See its assimilated forms e-, ef-, and es-. ex-is also used in the formation of English words such as "ex-partner," where it means "formerly having the status of."
The prefix al-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of ad-used before roots beginning with the letter "l," such as "loc" and "leg." See ad-.

Root_Definition: a person or thing that does
Root_Function: The suffix group -er, -or, -ar2turns verbs into agent nouns.

Root_Definition: state, quality, act, or practice of

Root_Function: The suffix -icattaches to roots and words of Greek or Latin origin to form adjectives. A few words ending in -ic(magic, critic, music) were adjectives that became nouns in Greek before they entered English, also as nouns.

Root_Definition: having or related to (a condition or state)
Root_Function: The suffix -oticattaches to Greek roots to form adjectives corresponding to nouns ending in "-osis."

Root_Definition: from, away from, off, off from

Root_Function: Most adjectives ending in "-ous," or "-ose1" can combine with "-ity" to form nouns ending in -osity.
The suffix -ory, -atory2attaches to Latin verb roots to form adjectives. Adjectives ending in "-atory" tend to have corresponding verbs ending in "-ate" (congratulatory: congratulate).
The suffix "-ous, -ious" attaches to Latin, Greek, and native English roots
The prefix "sus-" occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of "sub-."
The prefix suf-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of sub-used before  roots beginning with "f," such as "fus" and "fix." See sub-.

Root_Synonyms: proto, prot, arch, archi, arche (archae), archeo, (archaeo), -arch, -archy

Root_Function: See also -iferousand -fic

The suffix -ar1attaches to bound Latinate bases to form adjectives. Most adjectives ending in -ar1combine with the suffix -ity to form nouns ending in -arity. -ar1is a variant of -al2, -ial that for phonological reasons occurs with bases ending in 'l'.

The prefix ob-is a Latin preposition and prefix and occurs in English in Latin loanwords, such as object. It has multiple forms, as the 'b' sound in ob-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See its assimilated forms oc-, of-, op-, and o-.

Root_Definition: to cause to be or become or have
Root_Function: The suffix -en1forms verbs from monosyllabic English adjectives.

Root_Definition: person or thing that comes from, or is a member or follower of

Root_Function: The prefix suc-occurs in Latin loanwords. It is an assimilated form of sub-used before roots beginning with "c," such as "ced, ces, -ceed, -cede, -cess." See sub-.

The prefix re-occurs in verbs that are Latin loanwords, where it can mean "again"  (revise) or "back again" (reflect). It also attaches to English verbs (replay, rewind) with both meanings. Any verb can be prefixed by "re-" to indicate that an action is repeated. No hyphen is necessary unless the word formed is identical to an existing word (re-sign the document, but resignfrom a job).

Root_Definition: color, pigment; the element chromium or the substance chromatin

Root_Function: The suffix group -ance, -ence, -ency, -ancyattaches to verbs and Latin verb stems to create nouns. The suffix -anceis usually attached to whole English words, whereas -enceis usually attached to roots: compare eloquenceand acceptance. For most  nouns ending in -ance, -ence, -ency, -ancy, there is a correponsponding adjective form ending in -ant, -ent.

Originally a Latin preposition and prefix, ad-occurs in English in Latin loanwords. It has multiple forms, as the final 'd' sound in ad-assimilates to the initial sound of the base to which it is attached. See its assimilated forms: ac-, af-, ag-1, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, and at-.

Root_Definition: group (of a certain number indicated by the base)

Root_Function: The suffix -ism2has the same origin as -ism1but attaches to bases of diverse origins to form nouns denoting doctrines, beliefs, or theories. In the growing group of words modeled on the word "racism," -ismmeans "bias based on," as in "sexism" and "ageism." The majority of nouns ending in -ism2have a corresponding adjective and noun form ending in -ist.
The prefix oc-is an assimilated form of ob-used before roots beginning with "c." See ob-.
